newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - March 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - March 27.

text.p: Carter Holt Harvey's share price has dropped this year from a high of $3.40 to just $3.04 amid speculation that the company will issue new shares to help pay for a $1 billion purchase of the timber division of Australian giant conglomerate, CSR. The share price was already under pressure from lower commodity prices and moves by a major customer, Austalian-based packaging company Amcor, to cut the amount of linoboard it buys from CHH. Page 1.

Prudential on Wednesday won the race to buy NZI Life from General Accident plc, beating fellow bidders AMP, National Mutual and Tyndall Australia. The deal cost Prudential $163.3 million -- the highest price paid for a New Zealand life insurer in recent years. It was funded by Prudential's British parent. The move follows Prudential's announcement last week that it is relocating its funds management operation, Prudential Portfolio Managers NZ, to Sydney. Page 1.

Maori and Pakeha fishing interests again clashed in court this week, when it was claimed in the High Court at Wellington that Maoris' customary right to fish for snapper in the Hauraki Gulf should take precedence over the rights of recreational and commercial fishermen. When deciding quota cuts for the region, the government's first priority should have been Maori customary rights, the lawyer acting for several Maori groups told the court. Commercial fishermen should have been given second priority, with the interests of recreational fishermen coming in third, lawyer David Laurenson said. Page 3.

Dublin-based Independent Newspapers on Wednesday prepared the way to buy from New Zealand institutions the one percent to two percent of Wilson & Horton shares needed to reach its 90 percent compulsory acquisition target for the company. In a reverse offer, the Irish instructed brokers BZW to approach shareholder institutions asking them for indicative tenders of a price at which they would be prepared to sell. Page 3.

Jailed former Fortex managing director Graeme Thompson has aked the Attorney-General to re-open his file and conduct a special probe into the Serious Fraud Office's handling of the prosecution against him. In a letter from Rolleston Prison dated 14 March, Thomson urges Paul East, "in the light of recent revelations about SFO boss Chas Sturt's methods," to appoint a Queen's Counsel to investigate. In particular, Thompson raises the issue of the SFO's decision not to charge one of his colleagues with "essentially the same range of charges that were laid against me." Page 3.

United Water, this week's winner of the 50-year contract to run Papakura's water services, has been subjected to bribery and corruption claims relating to its A$1.5 billion water management contract with the South Australian Government. Labour MPs are accusing the state government of a massive cover-up after naming newly appointed state Premier John Olsen in fraud and corruption allegations. Olsen was responsible for striking the deal with United Water in late 1995. Page 4.

New Zealand's last remaining independent electricity retailer, Energy Brokers, will pull out of the retail business on 1 April, quoting poor -- or sometimes negative -- margins, and the difficulty of competing with local energy companies. Energy companies are able -- legally and sometimes possibly illegally -- to split overheads between their lucrative monopoly line businesses and the competitive energy retailing side -- an impossible situation for a retailer without a line business. Page 4.
